questions.q: According to this lesson, what does "a single data platform spanning multiple clouds" actually mean in practice?
options: Every table must have exactly one physical copy stored in exactly one cloud region worldwide
A consistent format, catalog, and governance layer across clouds -- not necessarily one single physical storage location for all the data
All compute engines must be retired in favor of a single vendor's engine
The term is purely marketing and has no real architectural meaning
questions.explain: The lesson's core point: 'single platform' describes a consistent format/catalog/governance layer, while the actual physical bytes can remain wherever data gravity or sovereignty requires them to be.

questions.q: What does an open table format like Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi actually provide?
options: A proprietary file format usable only by the vendor that created it
A networking protocol for connecting two clouds' virtual networks
A built-in encryption key management service
Database-like structure -- schema, transactions, time travel -- layered on top of plain files in cloud object storage, readable by multiple different compute engines
questions.explain: Open table formats add schema, transactional guarantees, and time travel on top of files in object storage, and the key payoff is that multiple compute engines (Spark, Snowflake, Trino, Athena, Fabric) can read the same underlying tables.

questions.q: What role does a catalog, such as Databricks Unity Catalog or the Iceberg REST catalog, actually play?
options: It tracks which tables exist, their schemas, and their permissions consistently across clouds and compute engines, which is what makes the platform feel singular
It physically stores all the data files in one central location
It replaces the need for any object storage entirely
It is only used for billing and has no role in data governance
questions.explain: The catalog -- not the storage bucket -- is what makes the platform feel singular: one governance model and table registry, even when physical bytes are deliberately scattered across clouds.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against having every compute engine read one single physical copy of all data across the public internet between clouds?
options: Because public internet access is always blocked by firewalls
Because it reintroduces the egress cost and latency problems from data gravity, and can directly violate data residency/sovereignty requirements
Because open table formats cannot be read over a network connection
Because catalogs only work within a single cloud account
questions.explain: Forcing all engines to read one physical copy across clouds reintroduces the exact egress cost and latency issues data gravity predicts, and can violate residency/sovereignty rules requiring certain data to stay in-region.

questions.q: What is deliberate regional/domain partitioning, as described in this lesson?
options: A method for compressing data before replication
A legal requirement that applies only to healthcare data
Splitting physical data by region or business domain so each cloud's compute serves its own local subset, rather than relying on one shared global copy
Randomly distributing data across clouds with no planning
questions.explain: Regional/domain partitioning deliberately splits data (e.g. EU customer data in an EU region, US data in a US region) so each cloud's compute serves the subset that's local to it, combined with table-level replication only for shared reference data.
